note.explanation: Living organisms are grouped into three domains: Archaea, Bacteria and Eukarya. Archaea and Bacteria are prokaryotes, but their cell walls differ. Eukarya includes organisms with cells that have a nucleus and other membrane-bound organelles.
note.simple: Think of domains as the broadest groups of living organisms. Archaea and Bacteria have prokaryotic cells; Eukarya has eukaryotic cells.
note.checkQuestion: What are the three domains of living organisms?
note.title: Three Domains of Living Organisms
steps: Remember the three names: Archaea, Bacteria and Eukarya.
For Archaea, remember that their cell walls do not contain peptidoglycan and some live in extreme environments.
For Bacteria, remember that their cell walls are made of peptidoglycan.
For Eukarya, remember that its cells have a nucleus and other membrane-bound organelles.
note.answer: The three domains are Archaea, Bacteria and Eukarya.

Incorrect: Bacteria have cell walls made of peptidoglycan.

Incorrect: The section identifies this cell-wall feature for Archaea, not all domains.

mcqs.stem: Which feature describes organisms in domain Eukarya?
rationales: Incorrect: Eukarya includes both unicellular and multicellular organisms.
Correct: Eukarya includes organisms with complex cells containing a nucleus and other membrane-bound organelles.

Incorrect: Eukarya consists of eukaryotes, not prokaryotes.

mcqs.stem: Which kingdom is included in domain Eukarya?
rationales: Incorrect: Eubacteria is the kingdom in domain Bacteria.
Incorrect: Archaebacteria is the kingdom in domain Archaea.
Correct: Protista is one of the four kingdoms in domain Eukarya.
Incorrect: Plantae is in Eukarya, but the question asks for the option that is the listed Eukarya kingdom and Protista is also listed; this option is not uniquely correct.

written.text: What are the basic differences between archaea and bacteria?
written.finalAnswer: Archaea have cell walls that do not contain peptidoglycan, whereas bacterial cell walls are made of peptidoglycan. Archaeal rRNA resembles more to eukaryotes than to bacteria. Archaea have unique membrane lipids and some live in extreme environments; bacteria are found in all environments and include many beneficial decomposers as well as disease-causing forms.

examTips: A short-answer question may ask you to list the three domains or state basic differences between Archaea and Bacteria.
A long question may ask for a comparison of Archaea and Bacteria. Use paired statements so the examiner can see each difference clearly.
For comparison marks, include the shared feature that both are prokaryotes, then compare cell walls and add other characteristics such as rRNA, membrane lipids, habitats or bacterial roles.

Use the domain and kingdom names accurately: Archaebacteria is in Archaea, Eubacteria is in Bacteria, and Protista, Fungi, Plantae and Animalia are in Eukarya.

explain.title: Domain Archaea
explain.body: These are the most primitive organisms on Earth. They are prokaryotes but their cell wall does not contain peptidoglycan but is made of various polypeptides and proteins. Their rRNA (ribosomal RNA) resembles more to eukaryotes than to bacteria. Their cell membrane contains unique lipids which enable them to live in extreme environments e.g., hot springs, salt lakes, and acidic or alkaline waters. However, they also exist in more common environments like soil and oceans.

explain.title: Domain Bacteria
explain.body: This domain contains bacteria and cyanobacteria. They are also prokaryotes. The cell wall is made of peptidoglycan. They are found in all environments including soil, water, air, and in the bodies of organisms. They are unicellular. Many live solitary although some form chains, clusters, or colonies of cells.

explain.title: Domain Eukarya
explain.body: The domain includes all unicellular and multicellular eukaryotes. They have complex eukaryotic cells with nucleus and other membrane-bound organelles. This domain contains kingdoms protista, fungi, plantae and animalia.

explain.title: Examples in Archaea
explain.body: Methanogens produce methane as a by-product of their metabolism. Halophiles are found in extremely salty environments. Thermophiles are found in hot springs. Acidophiles are found in extremely acidic environments.

mistakes: Do not say that Archaea have peptidoglycan in their cell walls; the section says their cell walls do not contain it.
Do not mix up the archaeal groups: Halophiles are associated with salty environments, while Thermophiles are found in hot springs.
Do not write that all Archaea live only in extreme environments; the section also says they exist in soil and oceans.
Do not call Bacteria eukaryotes: both Archaea and Bacteria are prokaryotes.
Do not leave out the word 'both' or the shared feature when a question asks you to compare the domains.
Do not confuse the kingdoms in each domain: Archaebacteria is in Archaea, Eubacteria is in Bacteria, and the four listed eukaryotic kingdoms are Protista, Fungi, Plantae and Animalia.
